sections.html:
Zanesville is the Muskingum County seat, about 52 miles east of Columbus, where the Licking River meets the Muskingum River. The population is 25,138. Renters outnumber owners here: owner occupancy is 43.8%, the median home value is $123,700, and median gross rent is $821.

With fewer than half of homes lived in by their owners, tenants are part of many sales. If your house has a tenant, tell buyers whether the lease runs past closing and who holds the deposit. Interstate 70 and U.S. 40 both run through town, which keeps commuters and travelers in the local buyer pool.

The city's Building and Code Enforcement office, at 401 Market Street, Room 227, enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, the city's codified ordinances and the zoning code. It can start legal proceedings against violators. Weekday hours run 7:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 740-617-4890.

The same office issues and inspects the permits a buyer's inspector will ask about:

  • Residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, which do not include plumbing.
  • Residential and commercial sidewalk, curb and curb cut permits.
  • Demolition permits.
  • Permits to move a house or an accessory structure wider than 14 feet or larger than 450 square feet.
  • Certificates of occupancy.

The office keeps lists of condemned properties and posts a 2026 annual vacant property form. If your house sits empty, ask whether the form applies to you before you list. For zoning questions, call Planning and Zoning at 740-617-4909. If your address is just outside the city line, South Zanesville has its own permit department at 740-454-0492.

sections.h2: Values, appeals and homestead in Muskingum County
sections.html:
The Muskingum County Auditor works from the courthouse at 401 Main Street, takes calls at (740) 455-7109 and keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. The January 2026 tax bills reflect values set in January 2025. An addition, a demolition or newly passed levies can change a bill.

Appealing your value

A three-member Board of Revision (the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president, or their designees) adjusts values. It has no say over tax dollars. A complaint is a legal filing, lodged with the auditor from January 1 to March 31. You can generally file once per three years, and withdrawing a complaint uses up your turn. What to expect:

  • Proof is on you, and the outcome can be a higher value, a lower one or none at all.
  • Certified mail brings the hearing notice at least ten days before the date.
  • After a filing, an appraiser from the auditor may visit and propose a settlement figure. Accepting it in writing cancels the hearing.
  • A corporation should have an attorney file for it.

Homestead exemption

The Homestead Exemption is for seniors, disabled owners and surviving spouses. For tax year 2025 it takes $29,000 off taxable market value, with an income limit of $41,000 that is adjusted each year for inflation. The filing deadline is December 31. A disabled-veteran owner gets a larger reduction, equal to the tax on up to $58,000 of market value. If you receive the exemption, ask the auditor how a sale affects it on your parcel.

sections.h2: What a Zanesville seller must disclose
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires every seller of a one to four unit home to complete a state disclosure form. Fill it in honestly and hand it over promptly. A seller is not liable for an inaccuracy that was outside the seller's actual knowledge. A buyer who receives the form late can walk away within three business days.

Gather permit numbers and any notices from the code office before showings, so the buyer sees them alongside the form. Open permits, a condemned notice or an unfiled vacant property form are the sort of loose ends that slow a closing.

sections.h2: Before you list: a short checklist
sections.html:
A few calls early in the process save time later. Start with the city code office to ask about permits for any addition, deck, furnace or panel replacement, and about the vacant property form if the house is empty. Then check with the county auditor about your value, the Homestead Exemption and whether the January bills reflect any recent change to the house.

Next, pull together the paperwork a buyer will want: the deed, any lease and deposit records if a tenant lives there, receipts for major repairs, and the permit numbers noted above. Complete the state disclosure form while the house is still on your mind, because a rushed form is where honest mistakes happen. If the house is vacant, walk through it for anything the code office could cite, such as overgrown yards, broken steps or boarded openings, and fix what you can before photos are taken.

If you plan to appeal, remember the window closes March 31. If you plan to sell before then, a successful complaint may still matter, since the result can follow the parcel. Ask the auditor how a pending complaint is handled when the property changes hands.

sections.h2: When a cash offer makes sense
sections.html:
Consider a cash offer for a rental with tenant trouble, an inherited house or a place whose repairs would worry a lender's appraiser. It can also end the monthly cost of a vacant house that keeps drawing taxes and utility bills. A cash sale generally skips the lender's appraisal and the repair negotiations that follow an inspection.

The usual steps are simple. You share the address and condition, an investor or buyer makes an offer after seeing the house, and you pick a closing date that suits you. A title company handles the paperwork and the deed transfer. Tenants, unpaid code citations and an incomplete permit history do not disappear in a cash sale, so settle what you can with the city first and be upfront about the rest.

Collect more than one written offer, compare closing costs and closing dates, and ask the title company for the settlement statement a day or two before you sign.

faqs.q: Who do I call about zoning in Zanesville?
faqs.a: Call the city's Planning and Zoning office at 740-617-4909. South Zanesville and several townships have separate contacts, since zoning follows the address.

faqs.q: How often can I appeal my Muskingum County property value?
faqs.a: Once in each three-year period, as a rule. Complaints are accepted from January 1 until March 31, and one that is later withdrawn still counts as your filing.

faqs.q: Can the Board of Revision raise my value?
faqs.a: Yes. The board may raise the value, lower it or leave it alone, and the burden of proof is on the owner. Bring a recent sale, an appraisal or repair estimates.

faqs.q: Does a vacant Zanesville house need to be registered?
faqs.a: The city posts an annual vacant property form for 2026. Call 740-617-4890 to learn whether your address must file before a sale.

faqs.q: What permits might a buyer ask me about?
faqs.a: A buyer's inspector may ask about residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, demolition permits and certificates of occupancy. All are issued by the city's Building and Code Enforcement office, so bring permit numbers for any addition or major system replacement.
